title: Western US Hydroclimate Scenarios Project Datasets
description:
This archive contains two datasets. Both cover the northwestern United States and part of southern British Columbia (N of about 38 degrees N and W of about 105 degrees W) at 1/16th (0.0625) degree resolution. Climate and hydrologic variables (21 total) in each are as follows: precipitation, temperature (avg./max./min.), outgoing longwave radiation, incoming shortwave radiation, relative humidity, vapor pressure deficit, evapotranspiration, runoff, baseflow, soil moisture (3-layers), snow water equivalent, snow depth, and potential evapotranspiration (5 vegetation references).
The first dataset, "Western US Hydroclimate Scenarios Project Dynamically Downscaled Data", contains daily dynamically downscaled climate projections and simulated land surface water and energy fluxes.  The downscaling is based on the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) regional model. WRF was run using boundary conditions from the ECHAM5 global model and the SRES A1B emissions scenario, one of the models from Phase 3 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP3), a critical source of data to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR4). Climate simulations were performed using an inner grid resolution of 12-km over the region and a 100-year (1970-2070) simulation.
The second dataset, "Western US Hydroclimate Scenarios Project Observations and Statistically Downscaled Data", contains daily statistically downscaled climate projections and simulated land surface water and energy fluxes for the western United States and southern British Columbia at 1/16th (0.0625) degree resolution. The downscaling used is the Modified Delta approach (see Littell et al. 2011), based on 10 models from Phase 3 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP3), a critical source of data to the Fourth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR4). Note that time-stamps on these data are not in the future.

title: iSnobal
description:
iSnobal is a physically-based distributed snowmelt model. Snowmelt is the principal source for soil moisture, ground-water re-charge, and stream-flow in mountainous regions of the western US, Canada, and other similar regions of the world. Information on the timing, magnitude, and contributing area of melt under variable or changing climate conditions is required for successful water and resource management. A coupled energy and mass-balance model iSnobal is used to simulate the development and melting of the seasonal snowcover in several mountain basins in California, Idaho, and Utah. Simulations are done over basins varying from 1 to 2500 km2 , with simulation periods varying from a few days for the smallest basin, Emerald Lake watershed in California, to multiple snow seasons for the Park City area in Utah. The model is driven by topographically corrected estimates of radiation, temperature, humidity, wind, and precipitation. Simulation results in all basins closely match independently measured snow water equivalent, snow depth, or runoff during both the development and depletion of the snowcover. Spatially distributed estimates of snow deposition and melt allow us to better understand the interaction between topographic structure, climate, and moisture availability in mountain basins of the western US. Application of topographically distributed models such as this will lead to improved water resource and watershed management.

title: Energy Use on Farms; Results from the Farm Business Survey
description:
These results cover the  physical quantities of inputs used on farm as well as the extent of farming practices such as use of contractors, minimal tillage and ploughing of grassland.
Source agency: Environment, Food and Rural Affairs
Designation: National Statistics

Alternative title: Energy Use on Farms; Results from the Farm Business Survey

Farm Energy Use: Results from the Farm Business Survey: England 2011/12

A statistical release covering farm energy use was published on 15/08/2013.  This workbook contains comprehensive data tables, including some not shown in the statistical release.

Link to main notice: https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/department-for-environment-food-rural-affairs/series/farm-business-survey#publications

If you require the data in a more accessible format, please contact fbs.queries@defra.gsi.gov.uk 

Survey details

Survey content and methodology
 
The Farm Business Survey (FBS) is an annual survey providing information on the financial position and physical and economic performance of farm businesses in England. The sample of around 1,900 farm businesses covers all regions of England and all types of farming with the data being collected by face to face interview with the farmer. To be eligible for the FBS, farm businesses must have a standard output of at least 25 thousand Euros.
 
In 2011/12 a sub-sample of around 200 farms in the FBS took part in an additional module to collect information on energy use.  The survey was designed to collect data for greenhouse gas calculations which will be reported on in late 2013.  Specific farm types were selected with a focus on those types which tend to have very dominant enterprises.  For this reason, horticulture, general cropping and mixed farm types were not surveyed.  It was also critical that full financial data was available for all responses, so the sample was restricted to those that completed that part of the FBS, although these represent over 90% of the full FBS sample.  The sample for cereals, dairy and grazing livestock farms was stratified into three strata, based on Standard Output.  This was not done for pigs and poultry farms.  The size breakdown of responses is close to the FBS population breakdown for some farm types but not for others.  
 
Full details of the characteristic of responding farms can be found at Appendix A.
 
Fuel volumes were converted into energy values (GJ) using factors extracted from the European Reference Life Cycle Database (ELCD) by Cranfield University.  These factors use a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) perspective which include energy used in the extraction, refinement and delivery of fuels, on top of the calorific value of the fuel itself.
 
For further information about the Farm Business Survey please see: https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/department-for-environment-food-rural-affairs/series/farm-business-survey
 
Data analysis
 
The omission of some farm types from this survey means that the results are not representative of the farming industry as a whole and no results are reported on this basis.  Due largely to the low number of observations, no attempt has been made to weight up results.  As such, results in this release should not be regarded as representative of the FBS population.  Extreme care should be taken when drawing conclusions from this release. 
 
Accuracy and reliability of the results
 
We show 95% confidence intervals against the results. These show the range of values that may apply to the figures. They mean that we are 95% confident that this range contains the true value. They are calculated as the standard errors (se) multiplied by 1.96 to give the 95% confidence interval (95% CI). The standard errors only give an indication of the sampling error. title: Interim London Energy and Greenhouse Gas Inventory (LEGGI) 2014
description: The London Energy and Greenhouse Gas Inventory (LEGGI) 2014 shows greenhouse gas emissions and energy consumption for London. This is an interim version of the LEGGI 2014, which will be confirmed when final data on energy use is published by the Department of Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) and Transport for London (TfL), expected in late 2017. The LEGGI shows estimates of energy consumption and carbon dioxide equivalent (CO 2 e) emissions from homes, workplaces and transport within the Greater London area. It is produced by the Greater London Authority on an annual basis to measure progress against the Mayor's Climate Change Mitigation and Energy Strategy. The LEGGI uses sub-regional energy (electricity, gas and other fuels) and CO 2 e data published by DECC/BEIS for homes and workplaces, and data from the London Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (LAEI) for energy and CO 2 e data for transport. DECC/BEIS E mission F actors (EFs) are used to estimate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from stationary and mobile sources of energy use in the LEGGI. These EFs are produced annually based on the national greenhouse gas inventory two years prior. E.g. 2016 EFs are calculated using national GHG emissions and energy use inventory data from 2014. So, for this 2014 LEGGI we have applied DECC/BEIS 2016 EFs to 2014 energy use to provide a more accurate estimate of GHG emissions in 2014 that is consistent with UK inventory data for 2014. We have retrospectively applied this method for EF selection to data from 2010 onwards to ensure consistency of approach and allow trends in CO 2 e estimates to be assessed. Interim results show that in 2014, London’s CO 2 e emissions were 37.8 million tonnes. This is a 16 percent reduction on 1990 levels and a 25 percent reduction since the peak of emissions in 2000. This is despite an ever-increasing population – an increase of 26 percent since 1990. London’s per capita emissions were estimated at 4.4 tonnes of CO 2 e in 2014, their lowest since 1990.

The monthly statistics for the Renewable Heat Incentive (RHI) programme present the number of applications and accredited installations on the scheme so far. The figures are broken down by technology type and GB region and application status.
The monthly statistics for the Renewable Heat Premium Payments (RHPP) scheme detail the number of vouchers issued and redeemed for the scheme so far. The figures are broken down by technology type and GB region. 

Note that from January 2015, RHPP figures are no longer be included in this release, and that from March 2016 the release will include quarterly data previously published separately.  Quarterly reporting introduced with effect from July 2022.

Final release published in April 2024 (March 2024 data).

Official Statistics

title: Space spectrum strategy
description: This document, published 1 Mar 2016, sets out Ofcom's proposed space spectrum strategy, which covers the use of spectrum by the satellite and space science (including earth observation) sectors. These sectors already deliver important benefits to UK citizens and consumers, such as broadcast TV, global positioning, communications to ships and aircraft, satellite imagery and information about our climate. There is potential for greater benefits in the future and we want to make sure we are focusing our efforts on the issues that will unlock the biggest benefits. We are inviting stakeholders' views on our analysis and our proposed priorities. Once confirmed, the strategy will shape the prioritisation our work in these sectors over the coming years. Alongside this document we are publishing a range of interactive data on use of spectrum by the satellite and space science sectors.

title: Workforce Management Information - Department of Energy and Climate Change
description:
"Monthly management information on staff numbers and paybill costs in Civil Service departments, their agencies and their executive NDPBs.
For workforce numbers, both payroll and non-payroll (contingent labour, including consultants) information is provided, split between full-time equivalents (FTE) and headcount, with payroll staff numbers mapped to standard Civil Service grades.
For costs, payroll paybill information is broken down into its component parts i.e. salaries, allowances, employers pensions contributions etc. For non-payroll costs, these are split between costs for consultancy and those of other non-payroll workers.
Staffing numbers are as at the last day of the month for the reference month. Cost information is that for the reference month. For baseline 2010/11 returns, staffing numbers are as at 31 March 2011, and paybill costs are for the financial year 2010/11."

title: 2017-18 Washington State CRDC Data - School Behavior and Climate
description:
The Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC) is a biennial (i.e., every other school year) survey required by the U.S. Department of Education’s (Department) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) since 1968. The CRDC collects a variety of information including student enrollment and educational programs and services, most of which is disaggregated by race/ethnicity, sex, limited English proficiency, and disability. The CRDC is a longstanding and important aspect of the ED Office for Civil Rights (OCR) overall strategy for administering and enforcing the civil rights statutes for which it is responsible. 

Data was reported directly from the school districts to the Office of Civil Rights. This data process is not managed by OSPI and therefore the data is not validated or reviewed by OSPI before being reported to OCR. For this reason data presented in this file will not mirror  OSPI reports on similar student and school measures.  The 2017-18 data in the report represents the most recent data made publicly available by the CRDC as of 5/10/2021.

In some cases data was unavailable or suppressed by OCR to protect student privacy, for more information on this please visit the CRDC webpage. In addition, directory information for some schools is incomplete, as the names of the organizations provided in the CRDC data files did not match the names of organizations on record with OSPI.

For additional information or questions about this data please visit the CRDC webpage at https://ocrdata.ed.gov/.

title: 2022 - 2024 NTD Annual Data - Fuel and Energy
description:
This dataset details fuel mileage and gallons/kilowatt hours for each agency, mode, and type of service (TOS) as reported by agencies submitted data to the National Transit Database (NTD) for the 2022, 2023, and 2024 report years. This file is based on the 2022 - 2024 Energy Consumption database files available at https://transit.dot.gov/ntd/ntd-data

Data Tables organize and summarize data from the 2022 - 2024 NTD in a manner that is more useful for quick reference and summary analysis. 

Only Full Reporters report energy consumption. Other reporter types do not appear in this dataset. Demand Response Taxi (DR/TX) mode and type of service combination does not report energy consumption and does not appear in this dataset. Finally, Non-dedicated fleets report energy consumption but not miles traveled. Thus for some agencies the given data for miles traveled are incomplete. Non-dedicated fleets represent about 7% of the data reflected in this dataset.

Please note that the column "Dual Fuel" was added in the 2025 report year. Values for 2022-2024 will thus be null.

In versions of the data tables from 2014-2021, you can find data on fuel and energy in the file called "Fuel and Energy" available from the NTD program website.

title: GHG Reporting Program Publication
description: This dataset contains greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions data reported to the Washington State Department of Ecology from the state’s largest emitters. As of 2022, this dataset accounts for the majority of the state’s emissions and serves as an indicator of the statewide total. Ecology separately calculates the statewide emissions total through the Washington State Greenhouse Gas Inventory. Reported emissions vs. Covered emissions Some of the graphs showing this data distinguish between the total emissions reported to Ecology by large emitters called reported emissions and the subset of that total that is covered by the Climate Commitment Act called covered emissions. Reported emissions • These are the total emissions from large emitters: facilities, fuel and natural gas suppliers, and electric power entities that emit 10,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (MTCO2e) or more annually. • These large emitters must report their emissions under WAC 173-441. Covered emissions • These are the emissions from a subset of large emitters that are regulated by the Climate Commitment Act (CCA): those that emit 25,000 MTCO2e or more of covered emissions annually. • This subset of large emitters is required to comply with the Climate Commitment Act under WAC 173-446. Notes • Emissions from biogenic fuels, as well as fuels used for agricultural, marine, and aviation purposes are exempt from the Climate Commitment Act under WAC 173-446-040. Because of this, some emitters’ covered emissions may be lower than their reported emissions. • To view data by reporter type, filter the Reporter Type column by Facility, Fuel Supplier, Natural Gas Supplier, or Electric Power Entity. Greenhouse gas emissions are in units of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalents (MTCO2e) using global warming potentials (GWPs) as specified in Table A-1 of WAC 173-441-040. History Ecology has been collecting reported emissions from Washington’s industrial facilities since 2012. In anticipation of the state’s major climate policies taking effect, the Legislature directed Ecology to collect emissions data from all large emitters in Washington starting in 2022 by expanding mandatory reporting to additional sectors: fuel and natural gas suppliers, and electricity importers. Reporting timeline • Before EY2022: Some large facilities began reporting emissions in EY2012. - Natural gas suppliers back-reported to EY2015 to establish a baseline. • EY2022: Additional fuel suppliers and electric power entities began reporting. • EY2023: The CCA Cap-and-Invest Program took effect. - Covered emissions are now being calculated. - Third-party verification is now required for entities that report more than 25,000 MTCO2e per year. Updates to the dataset • Ecology publishes emissions from the most recent emissions year annually. • Data from earlier years may be updated if reporters submit corrections that Ecology (and in some case, the third-party verification body) reviews and approves. Where to learn more • Mandatory greenhouse gas reports • Third-party verification (3PV) •

title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions
description:
The monthly Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emission data represents Montgomery County Facilities and Fleet by month beginning July 2019.  
Facilities: The Facilities GHG data represents physical structures used by County residents and County staff who provide services for County residents. Examples include recreation, libraries, theater and arts, health and human services, liquor retail, courthouses, general services, maintenance facilities, correctional facilities, police stations, fire stations, volunteer fire stations, garages, parking lots, bus shelters and park & ride locations. Facilities use the following fuel sources: grid electricity, natural gas, propane and diesel fuel. 
Facilities GHG data DOES NOT include Montgomery County Public Schools, Montgomery College and Montgomery Parks Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission (M-NCPPC). 
Fleet: The Fleet GHG data represents Montgomery County vehicles used by County staff who provide services for County residents. Examples include mass transit buses, snowplows, liquor trucks, light duty trucks, police cars, fire engines and fire service equipment, etc. Each County  vehicle use different fuel sources (i.e. diesel, mobil diesel, compressed natural gas, unleaded and E-85).  
Fleet GHG data DOES NOT include Montgomery County Public School buses, Montgomery College and Montgomery Parks Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission (M-NCPPC) vehicles. 
GHG Calculation Method: Facilities and Fleet fuel sources are converted into one common unit of energy- 1 Million British thermal units (MMBtu) which are then used with emissions factors and 100-year global warming potential (GWP) to calculate GHG emissions into one common unit of measure- Metric Tons of CO2 Equivalent (MTCO2e). 
For more information go to: 
•	How to Calculate GHG emissions at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zq5wTjvLqnY&t=186s
•	Emissions & Generation Resource Integrated Database (eGRID) at https://www.epa.gov/energy/emissions-generation-resource-integrated-database-egrid
•	Emission Factors for GHG Inventories at https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2018-03/documents/emission-factors_mar_2018_0.pdf

title: Residential Solar Investment Program (RSIP) Enrollment

Highlights
- $1.43B total investment
- $156M total incentive
- $0.41/W average incentive
- $3.79/W installed cost

How it works
- RSIP provided rebates and incentives to make rooftop solar more affordable for homeowners.
- When panels produce electricity, they save money and create Solar Home Renewable Energy Credits (SHRECs).
- Utilities entered into Master Purchase Agreements (MPAs) with the Green bank to buy SHRECs to comply with policy programs.
- Green bonds are created via SHREC revenue and purchased by both individual and institutional buyers.
- Revenue from MPAs and Green Bonds support RSIP incentives and cover administrative costs.

title: A 1 km gridded dataset of Northern Hemisphere permafrost active layer thickness (2000–2024)
description: This dataset provides annual active layer thickness (ALT) maps on a 1 km grid across the Northern Hemisphere permafrost region from 2000 to 2024. It was generated using a LightGBM–XGBoost ensemble trained with 2,373 quality-controlled annual ALT observations and multi-source climate, vegetation, topographic, soil, and biome predictors. The dataset includes annual ALT maps, relative site-resampling uncertainty layers, annual binary area-of-applicability (AOA) layers, and an AOA-frequency layer for 2000–2024. description: Abstract. title: Bandwidth-Invariant MTPA Speed Control of Induction Motor Drives With Application to Airborne Wind Energy Systems
description: Efficiency-oriented control of induction motor drives reduces rotor flux at partial load, but the resulting reduction in speed-loop gain degrades closed-loop bandwidth under fixed-gain control. The maximum torque per ampere (MTPA) constraint permits an exact resolution. Enforcing MTPA as a structural control law reduces the conventional two-input field-oriented-control plant to a single-input single-output system. Its linearized transfer function is a second-order plant with a real zero at twice the rotor-flux pole frequency. A gain-scheduled proportional-integral controller, whose gain is inversely proportional to the stator-current magnitude, cancels the operating-point dependence and maintains constant crossover frequency and phase margin without a flux observer or look-up table. Four strategies are compared in simulation and experimentally on an 18.5 kW induction machine under airborne-wind-energy pumping cycles: standard field-oriented control, fixed-gain MTPA, the proposed SISO-MTPA, and loss minimization. SISO-MTPA is the only strategy that improves both net harvested energy and speed tracking relative to the FOC baseline while remaining undominated: its energy is within 10% of the MTPA-optimal strategies, its speed-error RMSE is approximately 1.7 times lower, and its maximum deviation is over 40% lower. Against an industrial drive under high-power generation, it reduces speed-tracking RMSE by 47% with comparable generated energy. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23243453

title: COMPOSITE RISK INDEX AND EARLY DETECTION ALGORITHM FOR STRESS AND LOW-ENERGY INJURIES AMONG MILITARY PERSONNEL
description: Abstract.   Based on an examination of 220 military personnel aged 18–45 years, a composite risk index for stress and low-energy injuries was developed, incorporating 10 clinical, physical load-related, and bone metabolic indicators. The index demonstrated good discriminative performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.825 (95% CI 0.763–0.887), a sensitivity of 68.4%, and a specificity of 81.2%. Injury rates in the low-, moderate-, and high-risk groups were 7.1%, 23.5%, and 65.8%, respectively (p<0.001). A two-stage early detection algorithm was developed, comprising initial screening at the military unit medical facility followed by comprehensive assessment at a military hospital. The first-stage screening achieved a sensitivity of 94.7%, enabling the identification of military personnel at increased risk of injury before the onset of pronounced clinical manifestations. title: CURRENT STATE, TECHNOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT AND PROSPECTS OF SOLAR WATER STILLS: A CRITICAL REVIEW
description: This article critically reviews the current state, design solutions, heat and mass transfer mechanisms, and prospective development directions of solar-powered water desalination systems. In addition to conventional solar stills, the review covers phase change materials (PCMs), nanofluids, nano-enhanced PCMs, photovoltaic/thermal (PV/T) systems, external collectors, evacuated-tube heaters, thermoelectric modules, and hybrid desalination technologies. The literature indicates that the main advantages of conventional solar stills are their simplicity, low operating cost, and limited dependence on the electrical grid, whereas their principal limitations are relatively low productivity and strong dependence on solar radiation. Recent studies have achieved substantial productivity improvements through thermal energy storage, enlargement of the evaporation surface, enhanced condensation, and hybridization of energy sources. However, transferring high laboratory-scale performance to real operating conditions remains challenging because of the long-term stability of PCMs, environmental risks associated with nanomaterials, salt deposition, fouling, maintenance requirements, and the lack of comprehensive life-cycle assessment. For future systems, the article identifies the 4E approach—energy, exergy, economic, and environmental analysis—together with digital modeling and artificial-intelligence-based optimization as priority directions [1–8]. title: Can soluble organic fertilizers and/or manure reach the agronomic and environmental performance of synthetic fertilizers in drip-fertigated crops?
description: The substitution of synthetics by organic fertilizers, which is the current pillar of circular economy, has been broadly evaluated. However, varying results were obtained on nitrous oxide (N2O) and nitric oxide (NO) emissions as well as crop yields. Besides, in irrigated semi-arid croplands, drip fertigation has been suggested to be an effective practice for mitigating N2O and NO emissions while maintaining or enhancing agronomic performance. However, the promising combination of drip fertigation and organic fertilization remains poorly studied. By setting up melon (Cucumis melo L.) during 2022, and maize (Zea mays L.) during 2023, we aimed to evaluate the effect of different combinations of nitrogen (N) fertilizers: control without N fertilization, 100% of the N rate as solid manure (100OrM), 50% of the N rate as solid manure and 50% as urea (50OrM–50Syn), 50% of the N rate as solid manure and 50% as soluble organic (50OrM–50OrS), 100% of the N rate as urea (100Syn) and 100% of the N rate as soluble organic (100OrS). Urea and soluble organic fertilizers were supplied via drip fertigation. N-oxides (N2O and NO), methane (CH4) and ecosystem respiration (CO2) fluxes, mineral N (ammonium [NH4+] and nitrate [NO3−]), dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and crop parameters were analysed. As regards N2O, no differences were observed between treatments in melon crop, whereas in maize crop, the cumulative emissions were the highest in 100OrM, followed by 50OrM–50Syn. Regarding NO cumulative emissions, in the melon crop were significantly lower in 50OrM–50Syn and 50OrM–50OrS between 34%–54%, compared with 100OrM and 100Syn. In the maize crop, the highest cumulative NO emission was also detected in solid manure treatment. The agronomic response of melon to N fertilization was only detected for total soluble solids (with maximum values in the 100Syn treatment). The combination of solid manure and top-dressing urea or soluble organic fertilizer prevented the penalties in N use efficiency, which were observed in 100Syn and 100OrS. Therefore, the combination of conventional solid manure at seeding and soluble organic fertilizer at dressing (applied by drip fertigation) was the most sustainable strategy from agronomic and environmental viewpoints in Mediterranean irrigated agroecosystems. title: Climate and Geospatial Database of Jezero Crater, Mars: EPW Weather File and Environmental Data from the Mars 2020 Mission
description: This repository contains a climate and geospatial database for Jezero Crater, Mars (18.44° N; 77.45° E), developed to represent Martian microclimatic conditions in the  EnergyPlus Weather (EPW) format and support building energy and thermal performance simulations for space engineering and extraterrestrial architecture applications. The primary data were collected by the MEDA ( Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer ) environmental sensor suite aboard NASA's Perseverance rover during the Mars 2020 mission. The analyzed period covers mission sols 1–687, corresponding to approximately one Martian year. Repository structure The database comprises four main products: MARS_JEZERO_MEDA.epw  — A synthetic annual weather file containing 8,760 hourly records, constructed by sampling representative sols from the four Martian seasons and modeling the components of solar radiation. MEDA_selected_days_8760.xlsx — An Excel spreadsheet containing the hourly time series and meteorological variables integrated into the EPW file. MEDA_all_sols_hourly.xlsx — A tabular database containing raw and processed records of the environmental variables monitored by the rover during the analyzed period. Map_Location_Perseverance.png — A high-resolution map showing the landing site in Jezero Crater, local elevation data (-2,260 m to -2,648 m), and the rover's traversed route, with a cumulative displacement of 22.73 km. Sol selection and seasonal coverage To adapt the duration of a Martian year to the standardized EPW format, which comprises 365 days and 8,760 hours, uniform sampling based on linear interpolation of indices was applied, followed by a duplicate-removal procedure. Table 1 presents the distribution of the selected sols across the Martian seasons used to construct the synthetic annual weather time series.   Martian season Sol range Available sols Selected sols Mean interval (sols) Spring 0–182 168 102 1.65 Summer 183–360 164 99 1.66 Autumn 361–503 131 79 1.66 Winter 504–656 153 85 1.80 Total 0–656 616 365 1.69 Sensor characteristics and environmental variables Table 2: Meteorological variables were obtained using the MEDA instrument suite aboard the  Perseverance rover.   Sensor Unit Monitored variable or function Air Temperature Sensor (ATS) °C Air temperature measured at two heights: 0.85 m and 1.45 m. Pressure Sensor (PS) Pa Atmospheric pressure, with observed values ranging from 586.48 Pa to 819.98 Pa. Humidity Sensor (HS) % Relative humidity and sensor temperature. Radiation and Dust Sensor (RDS) W/m² Solar radiation flux and atmospheric dust properties. Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIS) °C Surface brightness temperature, thermal radiation, and albedo. Wind Sensor (WS) m/s, ° Wind speed and direction, with valid records available through sol 315. Data processing and modeling Solar radiation The solar radiation components — global horizontal irradiance, direct normal irradiance, and diffuse horizontal irradiance — were derived from RDS measurements combined with the SPICE toolkit and NAIF kernels to calculate the solar zenith angle ( θz\theta_z ). Direct radiation (B) was estimated using the Beer–Lambert law, assuming a constant dust optical depth ( τ=0.5\tau = 0.5 ). Diffuse radiation (D) was estimated using an isotropic scattering factor equivalent to 20% of the direct component. Wind patterns The anemometric profile records daytime and nighttime atmospheric circulation patterns. During the day, anabatic winds originating from the east were identified, associated with temperatures reaching -6.20 °C. At night, katabatic winds originating from the northwest were observed, associated with temperatures below -50 °C. Wind data are limited to the first 315 sols because of damage to the WS instrument. title: Data from: The legacy of past climate warming: strong local adaptation in rear-edge populations
description: Improving forecasts of species’ responses to climate change has become a central challenge in ecology and evolution as species distributions are increasingly disrupted by ongoing climate warming. Insight into this challenge may be gained through a better understanding of evolutionary responses to past climate change. The rear edges of species’ distributions are typically relict populations persisting in former glacial refugia at warmer range limits. As such, they form natural laboratories to study the evolutionary outcomes of past climate warming. Three such outcomes have been proposed for rear-edge populations: maintenance of high diversity due to long-term persistence, strong genetic drift following habitat decline, and strong local adaptation allowing persistence despite environmental change. Empirical studies rarely explicitly test these alternate outcomes limiting our understanding of evolutionary responses to warming climates. We tested all three evolutionary outcomes at the rear edge of the North American herb Campanula americana , by assessing genetic variation in a genome-wide population genetic study, drift load as measure of fitness decline due to drift in a controlled crossing study, and local adaptation in a transplant study. Rear-edge populations exhibited reduced genetic diversity within populations and high differentiation among populations, typically interpreted as evidence of genetic drift, yet show limited drift load. Instead, these populations expressed strong local adaptation, thriving in rear-edge habitats that were unsuitably warm for populations in the expanded range. This indicates that warm-edge populations may persist under warming climates by gradually adapting, even in the face of genetic erosion. Our findings highlight the importance of explicitly testing for all evolutionary outcomes, and particularly going beyond measures of genetic variation, when inferring evolutionary history. More broadly, these findings identify rear-edge populations not as relics of decline, but as underappreciated models for studying successful adaptation under long-term climate change. ECOLOGICAL DYNAMICS OF CRUSTACEAN ZOOPLANKTON AND THEIR CONTRIBUTION TO THE FOOD WEB OF TUDAKUL RESERVOIR
description: Crustacean zooplankton represents an important component of freshwater ecosystems and plays a significant role in the transfer of energy from primary producers to higher trophic levels. The present study considers the ecological characteristics of crustacean zooplankton inhabiting the Tudakul Reservoir, with particular attention to representatives of the classes Cladocera and Copepoda. The ecological importance of these organisms was assessed in relation to seasonal changes, environmental conditions, trophic interactions, and their contribution to the natural food resources of fish. Published data indicate that zooplankton communities of Uzbek reservoirs are composed of rotifers, cladocerans, and copepods, while Tudakul Reservoir has previously been reported to contain representatives of all three major groups. Crustacean zooplankton, particularly cladocerans and copepods, contributes substantially to the transfer of organic matter and energy within aquatic food webs. These organisms consume phytoplankton and particulate organic matter and, in turn, serve as food for fish and other aquatic consumers. The ecological significance of crustacean zooplankton in Tudakul Reservoir is therefore associated not only with its taxonomic diversity but also with its role in maintaining trophic interactions, supporting fish productivity, and responding to environmental changes. Monitoring the abundance and composition of Cladocera and Copepoda may provide useful information for evaluating the ecological condition and biological productivity of the reservoir. title: FROM AQUEDUCTS TO SMART WATER NETWORKS: THE EVOLUTION OF HYDRAULIC ENGINEERING
description: Abstract: Water management is one of the oldest and most persistent engineering challenges. Societies have always needed to collect, transport, lift, store, and distribute water while controlling losses and adapting infrastructure to local terrain and climate. This paper examines the historical development of hydraulic engineering from ancient irrigation and gravity-fed water systems to mechanized pumping and contemporary smart water networks. Using a qualitative historical-comparative method, selected technologies are evaluated according to four criteria: source of hydraulic energy, method of flow control, infrastructure function, and relevance to modern water engineering. The analysis shows that the history of hydraulic engineering is characterized by a gradual shift from passive use of gravity and landscape toward active control through mechanical devices, pressurized systems, powered pumps, measurement, and digital monitoring. Ancient canals and aqueducts established principles of gradient control and durable infrastructure; Greek and Roman technologies advanced lifting and distribution; engineers of the Islamic Golden Age developed sophisticated pumps and water-raising machines; industrialization made large-scale pressurized supply possible; and modern systems increasingly combine sensors, data analytics, leak detection, and automated control. The study argues that contemporary smart water infrastructure should be viewed as the latest stage in a long engineering process aimed at increasing reliability, efficiency, controllability, and resilience in the movement of water. title: Filtered SNP data for Climate Gradients and Habitat Discontinuity Structure Genetic Variation in a Spring-Specialist Plant
description: Climate gradients and habitat discontinuity structure genetic variation in a spring-specialist plant Dataset DOI: 10.5061/dryad.bk3j9kdtj Description of the data and file structure We collected tissue from plants from 17 populations of crimson monkeyflower from the Southwestern United States. Samples for each of these populations were collected from distinct sampling sites represented by a large spring or seep.  These sampling sites are identified by unique two letter codes throughout this manuscript with exact location information recorded for all sites.   Crimson monkeyflower populations are limited to landscape features that support perennial water sources, such as mountain ranges and riparian corridors. Our populations were collected from eight geographically distinct landscape features, including two mountain ranges (Huachuca Mountains and Black Mountains) and six riparian corridors (Gila River, Aravaipa Creek, Verde River, Oak Creek, Colorado River and Virgin River). For each population, leaf tissue from four to ten individuals was sampled for genetic analysis. We obtained 19 additional tissue samples from herbarium specimens from unique sampling locations allowing us to sample the southern portion of the range, resulting in a total of 189 samples. Tissue collections consisted of 2-3 leaves, which we dried in paper envelopes using silica gel.  We ground tissue using a FastPrep-24 homogenizer (MP Biomedicals) and extracted DNA from samples using a modified CTAB protocol (Doyle and Doyle 1987) with quality control performed using nanodrop and gel electrophoresis. We digested genomic DNA samples using EcoRI and MspI before ligating to adapters and indices as part of a reduced representation protocol (ddRADseq; Peterson et al., 2012) . We performed size selection using a Pippin Prep (Sage Science, Beverly, Massachusetts, USA) to select fragments between 400 and 600 bp. Samples were then pooled into a single library and sequenced at the Genomics and Cell Characterization Core Facility at the University of Oregon using a single lane of an Illumina NovaSeq 6000, SP 100 cycle run. Alignment and Genotyping We demultiplexed sequences using fastq-multx (Aronesty 2013) and completed sequence assembly and genotype calling using ipyrad (Eaton and Overcast 2020) . Raw reads were quality filtered to allow a maximum of 5 low-quality bases per read (Q < 20) and require a minimum read length of 35 bp after adapter trimming. Adapter sequences were removed, and reads were mapped to the Mimulus verbenaceus genome (MvBLg_v2.0; LaFountain et al. 2022) using a clustering threshold of 85% similarity. Consensus base calls required a minimum depth of 6 reads (both for statistical and majority-rule calling), with clusters exceeding 10,000 reads excluded. The datatype for assembly was specified as ‘ddrad’ for this assembly, with two restriction overhangs specified (AATTC, CGG). Initial variant calling produced a dataset of 150,710 loci across 189 individuals. We used VCFtools to filter this dataset to remove non-biallelic loci. Loci were further filtered to remove those with a minor allele frequency (MAF) ≤ 0.02 and those with ≥ 60% missing data. After filtering out low quality loci, missing loci per individual were calculated and used to filter out individuals missing > 60% of their data, in order to avoid bias in downstream analyses. High levels of missing data per individual can bias downstream estimates of heterozygosity and population structure (O’Leary et al. 2018) . Lastly, loci were thinned to one SNP per tag to reduce linkage among markers. description: This dataset provides a curated compilation of Ghana’s climate-related development finance and macroeconomic context, designed to support research on financing instruments, creditor composition, concessional lending and sovereign debt. The climate-finance component contains 2,719 OECD recipient-perspective commitment records covering 2000–2024. A cleaned version excludes one flagged exact duplicate, leaving 2,718 records across the full period and 2,587 records within the principal analytical window of 2010–2024. Records retain provider names, financial instruments, flow classifications, climate objectives, activity descriptions, amounts and source references. The compilation also includes 19 World Development Indicators series, with coverage extending back to 1983 where available; IMF financing-arrangement history from a snapshot dated 31 August 2024; Ghana Ministry of Finance public-debt observations preserved by report vintage; selected Green Climate Fund project approvals, instruments and disbursement events; and a documentary register, pilot evidence notes and qualitative coding protocol. Selected project and documentary material extends beyond 2024 and is identified as contextual evidence. It includes the original research workbook, CSV snapshots of all 18 worksheets, eight derived data tables, a data dictionary, methodological documentation, source-specific rights statements and file checksums. A Python reproduction script regenerates the cleaned records, annual and subperiod summaries, provider-coverage tables, concentration measures and robustness comparisons without external dependencies. All eight derived CSV files reproduce byte for byte. Climate-finance amounts represent reported commitments rather than national receipts, expenditure or sovereign liabilities. Provider coverage and climate-attribution methods vary across years. Missing values are preserved, overlapping public-debt vintages remain separate, and regional project totals are not assigned wholly to Ghana. title: Global CO2 emissions from cement production
description: GCP-CEM: The Global Carbon Project CEMent-process emissions dataset This is an update of the dataset documented in: Andrew, R.M., 2019. Global CO2 emissions from cement production, 1928–2018. Earth System Science Data 11, 1675–1710. https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-11-1675-2019 . Data in this release cover the period 1880–2025. title: Global map of Local Climate Zones
description: A global 100 m spatial resolution Local Climate Zone (LCZ) map, derived from multiple earth observation datasets and expert LCZ class labels. The LCZ map is based on the LCZ typology (Stewart and Oke, 2012) that distinguish urban surfaces accounting for their typical combination of micro-scale land-covers and associated physical properties. The LCZ scheme is distinguished from other land use / land cover schemes by its focus on urban and rural landscape types, which can be described by any of the 17 classes in the LCZ scheme. Out of the 17 LCZ classes, 10 reflect the 'built' environment, and each LCZ type is associated with generic numerical descriptions of key urban canopy parameters critical to model atmospheric responses to urbanisation. In addition, since LCZs were originally designed as a new framework for urban heat island studies (Stewart and Oke, 2012), they also contain a limited set (7) of 'natural' land-cover classes that can be used as 'control' or 'natural reference' areas. As these seven natural classes in the LCZ scheme can not capture the heterogeneity of the world’s existing natural ecosystems, we advise users - if required - to combine the built LCZ classes with any other land-cover product that provides a wider range of natural land-cover classes. title: Hygrothermal Aging Dataset and Performance of Thermoset Barrier Coatings for Infrastructure Longevity
description: Processed and derived data from an accelerated hygrothermal aging study of an epoxy barrier coating used for the rehabilitation of infrastructure. Coupons of a toughened epoxy composite were aged by dry-heat and by water immersion at four temperatures (20, 40, 60 and 80°C), for exposure periods ranging from an initial ~2-week sorption window to fourteen months of long-term gravimetric monitoring, and characterised by tensile testing (n = 5 specimens per condition), dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA; tan delta peak, ASTM D7028; n = 3 replicates) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC; first heating scan; n = 3 replicates), together with gravimetric water-uptake measurements. This dataset contains the derived/processed results reported in the associated manuscript: tensile modulus, strength and elongation at break across four aging conditions — dry-heat aging for two months; water immersion for two months, tested wet; water immersion for two months followed by drying, to assess the reversibility of property loss; and water immersion for four months, tested wet — each reported across the four aging temperatures. Glass transition temperature (Tg) by DMA and DSC after two months of water exposure showed a comparatively narrow range (DMA ≈ 30–36°C; DSC ≈ 31–36°C) despite close to a two-order-of-magnitude change in tensile modulus over the same temperature range, indicating that Tg alone does not capture the extent of hygrothermal degradation in this system. Initial sorption rate constants at each temperature, together with an Arrhenius fit of the rate constant (apparent activation energy ≈ 10.1 kJ/mol, R² = 0.98, over 20–80°C), and the long-term (to fourteen months) 60°C weight-change curve are also included; the latter shows weight gain continuing for approximately eight months (peaking near 35%) before a subsequent decrease, consistent with a transition from diffusion-controlled moisture uptake to degradation-associated water transport (swelling, leaching, or partial network dissolution) at prolonged exposure. The raw, coupon-by-coupon water-uptake, mechanical and thermal data are openly available in DiVA and are not duplicated here; see Related works and References for the full set of underlying and related records. P2P electricity trading: Participant configurations, bilateral trading connections, and associated operating parameters. Electric-drone mobility: Fleet characteristics, battery parameters, charging and discharging limits, mobility-distribution parameters, and stochastic scenario inputs. Scheduling and learning parameters: Hourly demand and renewable-generation profiles, electricity tariffs, scenario-generation settings, and deep reinforcement learning configuration parameters. The benchmark adopts a 24-hour scheduling horizon with hourly resolution. title: Kansas maize yield recovery under recurrent compound heat-drought events, 1981-2016
description: This dataset supports an observational spatial-panel analysis of maize yield responses and recovery following compound heat-drought events across 88 maize-growing grid cells in Kansas, United States, from 1981 to 2016. The deposit includes the processed climate and yield panel, compound-event indicators, event-onset and recovery-episode data, model outputs, sensitivity analyses, analysis code, data dictionaries, and quality-assurance documentation. Compound events were identified using cell-specific growing-season temperature and root-zone soil-moisture thresholds. The study evaluates immediate yield anomalies, multi-year recovery debt, repeated or persistent compound exposure, and robustness to alternative event definitions, detrending methods, covariance estimators, and percentile thresholds. Source datasets include GDHY maize yields, SAGE crop calendars, ERA5-Land temperature and soil moisture, and ERA5 precipitation. Users should consult the README and source-data documentation for variable definitions, provenance, and reuse conditions. Version 2 adds USDA NASS county-level total, irrigated, and non-irrigated maize yield and harvested-area records; the county-to-grid spatial crosswalk; irrigation-share construction files; yield-validation outputs; and irrigation-interaction and recovery-debt sensitivity results.   Version 3 (October 2026): This version adds supplementary data and code supporting the revised analysis of annual maize yield trajectories after compound heat–drought exposure. The addendum includes the archived USDA NASS corn-silking data and the reproduction workflow for Supplementary Table S11, the separate heat and drought severity analysis in Table S12, descriptive sensitivity results for the ±5% and ±10% two-season return criteria, and the data underlying Supplementary Figure S4. It also provides corrected return-time code that records the endpoint of the first qualifying pair of annual yield anomalies. This correction did not change the Cox model coefficients in the documented comparison. The original analytical packages and the Version 2 irrigation addendum are retained. The silking analysis is limited to years eligible under the archived USDA extract. Its reproduction workflow uses an archived intermediate dataset of qualifying compound-event days rather than reconstructing those days independently from raw daily climate data. The results describe annual yield trajectories and accumulated shortfalls under repeated exposure; they do not establish physiological recovery of the same maize crop. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23279840

title: Key Projects and Design Strategies in Energy-Efficient Contemporary Architecture
description: The built environment accounts for approximately 39% of global energy-related carbon dioxide emissions and over 36% of final energy consumption worldwide. In response to pressing climate imperatives, contemporary architecture has undergone a paradigm shift from conventional resource-intensive design toward ultra-low-energy, net-zero, and energy-positive building standards. This paper conducts a rigorous comparative analysis of iconic energy-efficient architectural projects utilizing the standardized IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) research framework. By evaluating landmark international case studies—including The Edge (Amsterdam), Powerhouse Brattørkaia (Trondheim), Bullitt Center (Seattle), Pearl River Tower (Guangzhou), and the Bahrain World Trade Center (Manama)—this study synthesizes the core mechanisms bridging passive architectural strategies (building orientation, high-performance thermal envelopes, natural ventilation) and active technological innovations (Building-Integrated Photovoltaics [BIPV], geothermal energy loops, and IoT-driven smart automation). Quantitative metrics demonstrate that the synergistic implementation of these approaches can achieve operational energy reductions exceeding 70% relative to regional baseline standards, while generating substantial surplus energy. Finally, the study evaluates technical, financial, and policy barriers and proposes actionable frameworks for adapting green building methodologies to hot, arid continental climates such as Central Asia. description: Abstract We characterized sediments recovered from the Alaska North Slope during the Collaborative Gas Hydrate Research and Development Project led by a consortium of the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC), U.S. Department of Energy (US-DOE), and U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). We analyzed core sediments for sedimentological, bulk geochemical, and rock magnetic properties. This project involved well logging, pressure coring, and a long-term production test at the Kuparuk 7-11-12 State well pad within the Prudhoe Bay Unit. Quantitative degassing (controlled depressurization) of a pressure core allows for measurement of the total volume of released gas in a core and characterization of the composition of the gas. Drilling operations of the HYDRATE 02 Geo Data Well (GDW) well occurred over 42 days between October 9 and November 19, 2022. The well location was located at 70 degrees 19' 1.84032" N and 149 degrees 12' 0.95289" W. The well was drilled to a total measured depth (MD) of 1084 m (3558 ft). Between 365 m (1199 ft) and the bottom of the hole, the well was drilled at an average inclination of 12.9 degrees with a maximum of 19.3 degrees. Eleven pressure cores (Cores 1P through 11P) were collected in the D1 sand and the overlying basal E shale between 722.07 m (2369.0 ft) and 755.78 m (2479.6 ft) MD. After scanning, the lithology of each core section was described and subsamples were collected for discrete sample analyses. These subsamples were analyzed via carbon-nitrogen-sulfur elemental and isotopic analysis, X-fluorescence elemental analysis, grain density measurements by gas pycnometry, and multiple rock magnetic techniques (room temperature, low temperature, high temperature). description: A complete description of the dataset is given by Jones et al. (2023) . Key information is provided below. Background A dataset describing the global warming response to national emissions CO 2 , CH 4 and N 2 O from fossil and land use sources during 1851-2024. National CO 2  emissions data are collated from the Global Carbon Project (Andrew and Peters, 2025; Friedlingstein et al., 2025).  National CH 4  and N 2 O emissions data are collated from PRIMAP-hist (HISTTP) (Gütschow et al., 2024). We construct a time series of cumulative CO2-equivalent emissions for each country, gas, and emissions source (fossil or land use). Emissions of CH 4  and N 2 O emissions are related to cumulative CO2-equivalent emissions using the Global Warming Potential (GWP*) approach, with best-estimates of the coefficients taken from the IPCC AR6 (Forster et al., 2021). Warming in response to cumulative CO2-equivalent emissions is estimated using the transient climate response to cumulative carbon emissions (TCRE) approach, with best-estimate value of TCRE taken from the IPCC AR6 (Forster et al., 2021, Canadell et al., 2021). 'Warming' is specifically the change in global mean surface temperature (GMST). The data files provide emissions, cumulative emissions and the GMST response by country, gas (CO 2 , CH 4 , N 2 O or 3-GHG total) and source (fossil emissions, land use emissions or the total). Data records: overview The data records include three comma separated values (.csv) files as described below. All files are in ‘long’ format with one value provided in the Data column for each combination of the categorical variables Year, Country Name, Country ISO3 code, Gas, and Component columns. Component  specifies fossil emissions, LULUCF emissions or total emissions of the gas. Gas specifies CO 2 , CH 4 , N 2 O or the three-gas total (labelled 3-GHG). Country ISO3 codes are specifically the unique ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes of each country. Data records: specifics Data are provided relative to 2 reference years (denoted ref_year below): 1850 and 1991. 1850 is a mutual first year of data spanning all input datasets. 1991 is relevant because the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change was operationalised in 1992. EMISSIONS_ANNUAL_{ref_year-20}-2024.csv: Data includes annual emissions of CO 2 (Pg CO 2 year -1 ), CH 4 (Tg CH 4 year -1 ) and N 2 O (Tg N 2 O year -1 ) during the period ref_year-20 to 2024. The  Data column provides values for every combination of the categorical variables. Data are provided from ref_year-20 because these data are required to calculate GWP* for CH 4 . EMISSIONS_CUMULATIVE_CO2e100_{ref_year+1}-2024.csv: Data includes the cumulative CO 2 equivalent emissions in units Pg CO 2 -e 100 during the period ref_year+1 to 2024 (i.e. since the reference year). The Data column provides values for every combination of the categorical variables.  GMST_response_{ref_year+1}-2024.csv: Data includes the change in global mean surface temperature (GMST) due to emissions of the three gases in units °C during the period ref_year+1 to 2024 (i.e. since the reference year). The Data column provides values for every combination of the categorical variables.  Accompanying Code Code is available at:  https://github.com/jonesmattw/National_Warming_Contributions . The code requires Input.zip to run (see README at the GitHub link). Further info: Country Groupings We also provide estimates of the contributions of various country groupings as defined by the UNFCCC: Annex I countries (number of countries, n = 42) Annex II countries (n = 23) economies in transition (EITs; n = 15) the least developed countries (LDCs; n = 47) the like-minded developing countries (LMDC; n = 24). title: Norway spruce shows stronger growth sensitivity and weaker intrinsic water-use efficiency response than Scots pine under increasing water limitation in southern Finland
description: The data supporting this study consist of tree-ring growth, stable carbon isotope, forest inventory, and climate records collected across southern Finland for the period 1990-2022. Tree-ring samples were obtained from six forest sites, including three Scots pine ( Pinus sylvestris L.) stands located on mineral soils and three Norway spruce ( Picea abies (L.) Karst) stands located on organic soils representing contrasting local moisture conditions. Annual basal area increment (BAI) was derived from dendrochronological measurements and used as an indicator of radial growth. Carbon isotope discrimination (Δ¹³C) was estimated and measured from d13c from annual tree rings and used to estimate intrinsic water-use efficiency (iWUE). To place site-level observations within a broader regional context, the tree-ring records were combined with species-specific growth indices (GIs) obtained from the Finnish National Forest Inventory (NFI). The NFI data represent regional growth dynamics across a wider range of sites and soil conditions than those included in the tree-ring network. Climatic drivers of growth and physiological responses were characterized using annual and seasonal climate variables, including vapour pressure deficit (VPD) and summer water balance. These variables were used to quantify atmospheric moisture demand and water availability and to assess their influence on interannual variability in BAI and iWUE. Site-level analyses incorporated local moisture conditions, whereas regional analyses focused on species-specific responses across southern Finland. The final dataset therefore includes annual observations of (i) tree growth expressed as basal area increment and NFI growth indices, (ii) carbon isotope discrimination and derived intrinsic water-use efficiency, (iii) climate variables describing atmospheric demand and water availability, and (iv) site descriptors including species, soil type, and relative moisture conditions. The dataset was designed to evaluate changes in growth and water-use efficiency under increasing water limitation and to compare species-specific responses across spatial scales ranging from individual forest stands to the regional forest inventory network. title: Pilot-scale integrated LCA and C-LCC analysis for sustainable active material selection in sodium-ion batteries
description: The sustainability of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) is strongly influenced by the environmental and economic performance of their active materials, particularly at early development stages. However, comparative assess- ments of multiple synthesis pathways under harmonized pilot-scale conditions remain limited. In this study, three Na0.7MnO2 cathode synthesis routes (solid-state, sol–gel, and hydrothermal) and three biomass-derived hard carbon anode production pathways (walnut shell via thermal treatment, corn straw via hydrothermal processing, and pomelo peel via chemical activation and carbonization) were assessed within a cradle-to-gate framework. Laboratory-scale data were upscaled to a pilot-scale production scenario (100 kg day 1) using a process-based scaling approach. Environmental impacts were quantified using the ReCiPe 2016 midpoint (H) method, while economic performance was evaluated through Commodity Life Cycle Costing (C-LCC) coupled with Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis.,The results reveal that process configuration and energy intensity dominate sustainability performance, outweighing the influence of raw material origin. Among cathode pro- duction routes, the solid-state method showed the lowest global warming potential (7.3 kg CO2 -eq kg 1) and median C-LCC (3.5 € kg 1), whereas the hydrothermal route exhibited significantly higher burdens (211.5 kg CO2 -eq kg 1; 124.2 € kg 1). For anode materials, pomelo peel–derived hard carbon presented the most favorable environmental and economic profile (57.6 kg CO2 -eq kg 1; 11.2 € kg 1), while corn straw–based production was strongly driven by electricity demand.,These findings identify energy and auxiliary material intensity as key drivers of sustainability and provide guidance for material and process selection in emerging sodium-ion battery technologies. title: Processed CMIP6 Earth System Model Carbon–Nitrogen Cycle Data
description: Overview This repository documents the processing workflow used to derive global annual carbon–nitrogen cycle data from original CMIP6 Earth system model (ESM) monthly output. The development of this dataset was motivated by the development of CNit (Carbon–Nitrogen Interactions in Terrestrial ecosystems; see  CNit documentation ;  Tang et al., 2025a ,  2026a ,  2026b ,  2026c ), the coupled carbon–nitrogen cycle model for MAGICC (Model for the Assessment of Greenhouse Gas Induced Climate Change; see  MAGICC repository ;  Meinshausen et al., 2011 ). During the processing and analysis of ESM output, we identified notable mass-conservation issues that prevented the direct calibration of CNit, which strictly conserves carbon and nitrogen mass. Through investigations involving ESM teams and analysis of the model output, we found that these issues are related to the way carbon and nitrogen pools and fluxes are reported in ESM output. Based on these findings, we have provided recommendations for future data providers, data users, and different MIPs. Further details are provided in  Tang et al., (2025b)  and the accompanying  community technical report . The processed dataset ( 17 ESMs across the 1pctCO2 series, historical, and SSP scenarios ) can support a range of applications, including calibration and evaluation of simple climate models (SCMs) at both spatially resolved and global-integrated scales, intercomparison of terrestrial carbon–nitrogen cycle states and fluxes across ESMs, analysis of carbon–nitrogen cycle responses across experiments and scenarios, and evaluation of model consistency and mass conservation. The dataset also provides a standardized annual-resolution basis for analysing the variation and temporal evolution of terrestrial carbon and nitrogen pools and fluxes across CMIP6 ESMs.   Changelog 2026-10-08 — Initial upload Added README.ipynb : A notebook documenting the background, data processing and correction procedures, and data distribution. Added notebooks.tar.gz and  environment.yml : Source code and the environment file for reproducing the data processing workflow. Added land_area_related.tar.gz : Multiple .pkl files containing ESM-specific grid area, land fraction, and land area data . Added global_annual_data.tar.gz : A single NetCDF file,  CMIP6_ESM_carbon_nitrogen_cycle_outputs_global_annual_processed_by_Gang_Tang.nc , containing global land-integrated annual data for all ESMs and experiments .    Added annual_data.tar.gz : Multiple NetCDF files containing gridded annual data for each model–experiment combination . This file is not provided here because of difficulties uploading the large global gridded annual data to Zenodo. Instead, it is available from Figshare (link: https://doi.org/10.26188/34089963 ). description: This dataset is the replication package for “Embodied Carbon Liability: Value Added, Not Gross Output” (W.-T. Fang, submitted to Ecological Indicators). The first-arrival arrays permit independent recomputation of arrival mass, kinetic energy, energy per arriving mass, and the contributions of shared and condition-specific particle identities. title: Supporting information for "Global and regional Pleistocene benthic δ18O stacks on age models with and without astronomical tuning"
description: Note: The BIGSTACKs are in the file "Zhou et al_Supplementary_data_files.xlsx". Constructing accurate age models for Pleistocene marine sediments is crucial for our understanding of glacial-interglacial cycles and other climatic processes. Benthic foraminiferal δ 18 O stacks, a proxy for ice sheet and climate evolution, are often used for stratigraphic alignment and chronology development in deep-sea sedimentary records, in combination with biostratigraphy, paleomagnetism, and radioisotopic constraints. Selection of an appropriate benthic δ 18 O alignment target influences the derived chronology at a given site, and divergent regional trends in benthic δ 18 O highlight the need for ocean-specific benthic δ 18 O stacks. The specific scientific question to be addressed by a study may also influence whether the alignment target should include astronomical tuning. Here, we introduce three benthic δ 18 O stacks – Atlantic, Pacific, and global – with three distinct chronologies for the global stack that incorporate astronomical forcing constraints to various degrees. The new global stack utilizes data from 224 cores and includes 50% more data than the previous “ProbStack” (Ahn et al., 2017). Hand-tuned regional and global stacks, intended as updates to the “LR04” stack (Lisiecki and Raymo, 2005), incorporate chronologies transferred from absolutely dated archives during 0-654 thousand years ago (ka) and an astronomically forced ice sheet model during 654-2700 ka. Due to the heterogeneous nature of the age constraints used for these stacks, we call them BIGSTACK mixed , BIGSTACK mixedA , and BIGSTACK mixedP . For applications where astronomical tuning should be minimized, we present a global stack primarily constrained by geomagnetic reversal age estimates, BIGSTACK magrev . We also develop a third age model, BIGSTACK auto , which uses an automated optimization algorithm to “minimally tune” the stack to the pervasive ~41 kyr obliquity cycle, while avoiding assumptions about astronomical phase relationships. This suite of stacks offers flexibility in choosing δ 18 O stratigraphic alignment targets, to allow a wide range of applications in paleoceanographic hypothesis testing. Feb. 10th, 2026 update : the gap of NaN values in BIGSTACK mixed should be 645-650 ka, but in the previous version was 10 kyrs longer (635-650 ka) by mistake. The reason for a gap in the stack during that period is still valid — it's where two portions of the stack, based on absolutely dated targets (0-650ka) and astronomically tuned ice volume modeling (>650 ka), are joined together. Oct. 7th, 2026 update : we present a new version of BIGSTACK magrev that updates the age of the Brunhes/Matuyama boundary to 773 ka (Suganuma et al., 2018; Singer et al., 2019). We thank Prof. Brad Singer for bringing to our attention the evidence pointing to 773 ka as the boundary age. Other BIGSTACKs remain the same as the last version. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23220134

description: The Navoi Region of Uzbekistan possesses significant tourism potential determined by its distinctive physical-geographical characteristics, including extensive desert landscapes, geological formations, mountain systems, natural water bodies, unique ecosystems, and a continental climate. The region occupies an important position in the central part of Uzbekistan and includes the Kyzylkum Desert, the Nuratau Mountains, the Zarafshan River valley, and several areas of ecological and landscape significance. These natural conditions create opportunities for the development of ecological, recreational, adventure, geological, landscape, and nature-based tourism. This review examines the principal physical-geographical factors influencing tourism development in the Navoi Region, with particular attention to relief, climate, hydrology, landscapes, biodiversity, and the spatial distribution of natural recreational resources. The study demonstrates that a geographical approach to tourism planning can contribute to the rational use of natural resources, diversification of tourist routes, and sustainable development of tourism in the region. title: The Global Carbon Project's fossil CO2 emissions dataset
description: The Global Carbon Project (GCP) has been publishing estimates of global and national fossil CO2 emissions since 2001. In the first instance these were simple re-publications of data from another source, but over subsequent years refinements have been made in response to feedback and identification of inaccuracies. In this article (PDF document) we describe the history of this process leading up to the methodology used in the 2025 release of the GCP's fossil CO2 dataset. The fossil CO2 emissions dataset is included in both its standard, absolute form, and per capita, with associated metadata files in JSON format. A file indicating the source(s) of each data point is also provided. This is the initial release of the 2025 dataset. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.17417124

title: Toward Intelligent and Climate-Resilient Coastal Aquaculture: A Systematic Review Integrating Ecosystem Health, Marine Biotechnology, One Health, Data-Driven Technologies, and the Blue Economy
description: This repository contains the underlying and extended data supporting the systematic review “Toward Intelligent and Climate-Resilient Coastal Aquaculture: A Systematic Review Integrating Ecosystem Health, Marine Biotechnology, One Health, Data-Driven Technologies, and the Blue Economy.”   The repository contains the strict 261-study evidence map used for manuscript-level quantitative summaries and thematic synthesis; study-level bibliographic and descriptive characteristics; study-level methodological appraisal results; the complete Scopus and PubMed search strategy and query provenance; the full-text exclusion log; the completed PRISMA 2020 checklist; the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram; and the final verified PRISMA count audit.   The strict synthesis includes 261 full-text-verified studies allocated across six research domains: RQ1 (n = 25), RQ2 (n = 70), RQ3 (n = 32), RQ4 (n = 53), RQ5 (n = 50), and RQ6 (n = 31). Artificial light at night (ALAN)/light pollution was not retrospectively added to the database search strategy and is treated only as an emerging synthesis theme and evidence gap.   The deposited materials are intended to support transparency, reproducibility, verification of the systematic-review workflow, and reuse of the study-level evidence base. title: Viçosa Urban Microclimate Weather Dataset: EPW Files Based on Local Measurements and Future Climate Scenarios
description: This repository contains a collection of weather files in EnergyPlus Weather (EPW) format developed to represent the urban microclimatic variability of Viçosa, Minas Gerais, Brazil, as well as future climate projections. A key characteristic of the baseline files is that they are stitched (synthetic) annual weather series (8,760 hours) created by integrating hourly regional meteorological data from the National Institute of Meteorology (INMET) with high-resolution, local microclimatic measurements of air temperature and relative humidity. Local measurements were obtained across 16 strategic urban points using automated Onset HOBO thermo-hygrometers during three seasonal field campaigns (Winter 2025, Spring 2025, and Summer 2026). For hours outside these specific field campaigns, reference data from the INMET station were retained to complete the full annual cycle. title: When Twin Transitions Compete: AI Acceleration, Digital Absorptive Capacity, and Renewable-Capacity Expansion in the European Union
description: This replication package contains the analytical data, R code, intermediate outputs, robustness diagnostics, figures, and documentation supporting the study “When Twin Transitions Compete: AI Acceleration, Digital Absorptive Capacity, and Renewable-Capacity Expansion in the European Union.” The study examines the EU-27 over 2015–2025 and evaluates whether economies with greater predetermined digital absorptive capacity experienced different renewable-capacity trajectories during the post-2022 acceleration in artificial intelligence. The package supports reproduction of the principal two-way fixed-effects models, event-study estimates, post-2022 differential-exposure specifications, placebo tests, alternative exposure and outcome models, mechanism tests, leave-one-country-out analysis, geopolitical sensitivity tests, and wild-cluster-bootstrap inference.   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23272193
